analysis.one_liner: Requires large tax-exempt hospitals to disclose charity care, finances, and drug-discount profits to the IRS.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee voted 25–15 to advance a bill requiring tax-exempt hospitals to disclose their charity care, finances, and 340B drug-discount margins, but the full House has not voted and the congressional session ends January 3, 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require tax-exempt hospitals to tell the IRS, on their public filings, how much financial assistance they actually gave, how many aid applications they granted or denied, which community health needs they left unaddressed and why, and their audited financials. Hospitals with more than 100 beds or more than $100 million in patient revenue would have to break this down facility by facility and also report profits by service line, advertising spending, and their margins from the 340B drug discount program. It also directs the Government Accountability Office to estimate how much tax the 25 largest tax-exempt hospitals would pay if they lost their exemption.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, donors, and taxpayers, who would see — hospital by hospital, and for large systems facility by facility — how much charity care tax-exempt hospitals actually deliver, how many financial-assistance applications they deny, how much they spend on administration and lobbying-adjacent functions versus care, and how much they profit from the 340B drug discount program. Congress would also get data on what the largest tax-exempt hospital systems would owe in taxes if they were not exempt.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every tax-exempt hospital to report on its IRS return the value of financial assistance provided and the number of completed aid applications received, granted, and denied, so communities can see whether hospitals are earning their tax exemption.
Requires hospitals to describe how they are addressing the health needs identified in their community health needs assessment — and to name the needs they are not addressing and explain why.

Requires large hospitals (more than 100 staffed beds) and high-revenue hospitals (more than $100 million in net patient revenue) to report separately for each facility they run, so problems at specific hospitals cannot be hidden inside a system-wide average.

Requires high-revenue hospitals to disclose revenue and costs for each health service line, allowable and unallowable advertising costs, and spending on nonclinical programming such as administration, billing, government affairs, and lobbying — exposing how much goes to care versus overhead.

Requires high-revenue hospitals that participate in the 340B drug discount program to report how many patients received discounted drugs and their aggregate net 340B payments, making visible the profit hospitals capture from the program.

Directs the GAO to report the compliance costs of the new requirements and to estimate how much tax the 25 largest tax-exempt hospital organizations would pay if their exemption were lifted, giving Congress data for any future debate over taxing them.

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt hospitals — especially large, high-revenue systems — bear the cost: they must produce audited financial statements, count and value financial assistance, break data down by facility, map their internal service lines to a new federal taxonomy within two years (bearing the burden of proof if they claim a cost center is not a service line), and disclose 340B margins and advertising costs. The Treasury Department absorbs administrative costs, and taxpayers fund the GAO study. Some hospitals may pass compliance costs on through prices.

drawbacks.text: The reporting burden is heavy and technical: high-revenue hospitals must map their internally defined service lines to a standardized federal taxonomy within two years, allocate shared costs among them, and prove their case if they assert a cost center is not a service line — a real accounting and legal cost for hospitals, which the bill itself anticipates by ordering a GAO study of compliance costs.

The bill is disclosure only. It forces hospitals to reveal charity care gaps and 340B profits but does not require them to give more assistance or change 340B practices — the text expressly states it creates no inference about the proper application of the 501(r) charity care rules or the 340B program — so publication alone may not change hospital behavior.

Compliance costs could be passed on to patients and payers through higher charges, and the government bears added administrative costs; the GAO is directed to measure both before anyone can judge whether the transparency was worth it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuine but indirect benefit: the bill gives patients, donors, and Congress the data to judge whether tax-exempt hospitals deserve their exemption, without forcing any hospital to change behavior. The main honest cost is the compliance burden — facility-level and service-line accounting to a new federal standard — which the bill wisely exempts from small rural providers (critical access and rural emergency hospitals) and phases in over several years, and which it directs the GAO to measure. A reasonable trade if it leads to real scrutiny of the largest systems; weak if the data is published and nothing follows.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared committee on a 25–15 vote but has never come up for a vote by the full House, and the current congressional session ends January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Murphy (R-NC) introduced the bill on June 29, 2026, with Rep. Lloyd Smucker as cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax law.
Two days later, on July 1, 2026, the committee held a markup and voted 25–15 to order the bill reported with a substitute version, meaning a rewritten version moved out of committee.
No further action has been taken: the bill has not received a vote by the full House, and the Congress ends on January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won yet. If the bill stalls, large tax-exempt hospital systems come out ahead because they avoid facility-level, service-line, and 340B disclosure of their finances.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large tax-exempt hospital systems, if it stalls

sides.party_line_note: The record does not break down the 25–15 committee vote by party; the sponsor and its one cosponsor are both Republicans, and no floor vote has occurred.

industries.note: Hospitals with more than 100 staffed beds or more than $100 million in net patient revenue must report their finances, charity care, and service-line profits facility by facility, including how much they spend on administration, advertising, and lobbying versus care. This exposes whether tax-exempt hospitals earn the billions in tax breaks tied to their charitable mission, which is exactly the scrutiny they have an interest in avoiding.

High-revenue hospitals must disclose their aggregate net 340B payments — the profit margin they capture between discounted drug prices and what insurers pay — plus the costs of running the program. Disclosure of these margins strengthens arguments for reining in 340B hospital profits, which hospitals benefit from today.

Drug makers supply discounted drugs under 340B and have long argued hospitals pocket the difference; the new hospital-side margin data gives them evidence for that argument. The bill itself changes nothing about drug pricing, so the gain is informational, not financial.
Hospitals must attach audited financial statements and build new cost-accounting to map service lines to a federal taxonomy — work that flows to audit and consulting firms.

analysis.trajectory: Bills reported out of committee in the final months of a session rarely reach the floor on their own. Unless House leadership schedules a vote or the provisions are folded into a larger tax bill, H.R. 9504 will likely expire when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, and would have to be reintroduced next year.
